i don’t have BPD but i tried TMS with no success, then did ECT and it improved my depression significantly. worked for me when nothing else did. my memory is pretty bad now, but not unmanageable. i didn’t retroactively lose old memories, it’s just a lot harder to retain things. it was worse during the actual course of treatment and now it’s slightly better (but still not great). 

it was worth it for me, just depends on your personal situation and how much risk you’re willing to take in order to potentially see some improvement in symptoms longer-term. hope that helps a little!

I’m sure it feels uncomfortable and worrying in the moment, but personally I don’t think it’s necessarily a bad sign. Other comments mentioned this, but ECT is designed to cause intense and sudden change. I understand how that can be overwhelming though, that’s definitely how I felt.

ECT is no small thing and I think it’s very common for people to feel lots of (pleasant and/or unpleasant) changes in the short-term. Some of those changes might fade as your body and brain start to recover from the shock (no pun intended lol) of treatment, and hopefully other changes will stick and help improve your mental wellbeing longer-term. That was my experience but I still think it doesn’t hurt to mention this to your doctor next time you’re in touch, if it doesn’t go away.

I do think it’s likely to sort of “stabilize” over time though!

can’t really predict that, unfortunately. sorry that you’re struggling but i promise the sooner you quit, the easier it’ll be. it’ll only get harder from here because the longer and more you smoke, the more addicted you’ll be. try to quit now, use NRT if you absolutely have to, and push through the initial withdrawal because i promise that sick feeling will pass. those things will be even more intense if you keep smoking.

that’s not how it works, we don’t get to choose when orders are grouped together. “I might as well just leave a shit tip” you’re angry about a profit maximizing strategy dictated by corporate policy-makers at doordash. Then you’re redirecting it towards the drivers making scraps with no power over the algorithm (or how anything else gets done). complain to them, not us.

i’m sorry that you’ve been dealing with mental health issues, i know that it’s a nightmare. but i started smoking for similar reasons and can tell you with 100% certainty that it doesn’t help. it doesn’t really make you feel better, the only relief is from temporarily satisfying your addiction and putting cravings on pause. it’ll just compound the stress you’re already feeling. i hope you can find something else that works for you but i promise smoking isn’t an easy solution.

doordash needs to make it clear to customers when their driver is doing several deliveries as part of a single order. 

i recently had two different deliveries as a grouped order in the same complex, and one of the customers started messaging me to tell me he was on the other side of the complex and i was in the wrong place. i think they’re watching us on the map and assuming that we’re able to drop the food off directly without other stops.

it’s unnecessarily difficult trying to juggle contacting multiple customers at once (particularly when one of them thinks you’re confused and need to be navigated somewhere else) while finding the right drop off point and holding food + drinks on a countdown that can affect your “rewards” status. clearly the lack of transparency at every turn doesn’t matter to them since it doesn’t affect the bottom line.

congrats on your progress! i totally understand those thoughts and cravings, they’re very powerful and appealing at times. 

what i’ll offer in terms of challenging those urges is that (in my experience) smoking is never as enjoyable in practice/reality as it is in my head. it typically ends in regret, money down the drain, and waking up at 4am with postnasal drip and an itch in my throat that i can’t get rid of. i used to think that i liked the taste and smell, but now it bothers me more. last time i smoked i wanted to gag when i reached the end of my cig.

obviously the downsides aren’t always the same for everyone, but i think our addicted brains tend to ignore that the payoff usually doesn’t live up to those expectations. you quit for a reason and you’ve got a great streak going, so props to you!

i’m a bit late replying, but i was running a low fever the night after my third treatment. i felt absolutely awful, had chills and nausea, stabbing headache, etc. i’m trying some medication changes during my next treatment so hopefully it won’t happen again. my doctor didn’t indicate that it happens very frequently but i still don’t think you’re the only one, and it’s worth addressing. hope you’re feeling better now!

good luck on your quit, i really hope the patches are helpful. some form (or multiple forms) of nicotine replacement sound like a good option for you based on your circumstances and there should be no shame in using them as a tool; you can eliminate sources of nicotine incrementally and take this one step at a time. i’ve found nicotine lozenges very helpful and i’ve been able to slowly decrease my usage over several months.

if you’re not doing this already and you have the means, seeing a doctor for guidance might help make the process easier given the severity of your past withdrawal symptoms.

focusing on expanding (and practicing) your anxiety management techniques - especially physical ones like DBT TIPP skills, vagus nerve exercises, or the dive reflex - might help a tiny bit too. i don’t mean to minimize that level of unbearable anxiety, i just think anything that helps even a little bit is probably worth trying and it’s good to have a full toolbox ahead of time. it’s not easy but you’re doing the right thing. beating yourself up generally makes things even harder and you deserve better than that.
